Sinaloa Cartel · Mexico

The oldest continuously operating Mexican trafficking organisation, and since the 2016 extradition of Joaquín Guzmán the subject of an internal war between the faction around his sons ("Los Chapitos") and that around Ismael Zambada ("La Mayiza"). Zambada's capture in Texas in July 2024, which he says followed an abduction by one of Guzmán's sons, triggered open fighting in Sinaloa state. Designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization in February 2025. Its capture reach is the best-documented of any group here: the conviction of Genaro García Luna, Mexico's former security minister, rested on payments from this organisation.

fa17b1966bc4d26a.h:
Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC)

Prison-born organisations · Brazil
PCC · Brazil

Founded inside São Paulo's prison system in 1993 and now assessed as Brazil's largest criminal organisation, with a membership structure, dues, and an internal court. Its expansion followed the prison network rather than territory, which is why it reaches Paraguay and Bolivia. Brazilian and Paraguayan investigations have repeatedly reached prison staff and police; the 2022 A Ultranza Py operation in Paraguay implicated senior officials in a laundering network tied to it. Designated a Specially Designated Global Terrorist by the United States in May 2026, with Foreign Terrorist Organization designation effective 5 June — the liability falls chiefly on companies, since material support is defined broadly enough to reach counterparties dealing entirely outside the United States.

480afcca1f904bde.h:
Tren de Aragua

Prison-born organisations · Venezuela/USA
Tren de Aragua · Venezuela

Originated in Venezuela's Tocorón prison, which its leadership ran openly — with a pool, a zoo and a nightclub — until the government retook it in September 2023. Its expansion followed Venezuelan migration routes across the Americas. Designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the United States in 2025. Note that US claims of Venezuelan state direction have been publicly contradicted by parts of the US intelligence community, and remain contested.

US Treasury OFAC; US FTO designation 2025; Venezuelan government Tocorón operation, Sept 2023; US NIC assessment reporting, 2025

Placed at: Doral / Sweetwater, Miami-Dade — the diaspora presence

7d0602fad26656ed.h:
Los Choneros

Prison-born organisations · Ecuador
Los Choneros · Ecuador

The organisation at the centre of Ecuador's collapse from one of the region's safest countries to one of its most violent. Its leader José Adolfo Macías escaped from prison in January 2024, prompting the declaration of an internal armed conflict. The Metástasis case, carried in this map's state-case layer, arose from decrypting a trafficker's phone and reached judges, prosecutors and prison officials tied to this network. Designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization and Specially Designated Global Terrorist in September 2025, alongside Los Lobos; its leader José Adolfo Macías was extradited to the United States in July 2025, the first Ecuadorian citizen extradited from Ecuador.

Ecuadorian Fiscalía General, Caso Metástasis, from Dec 2023; Ecuadorian state of exception decrees; US Department of State terrorist designations, 4 September 2025

Placed at: Penitenciaría del Litoral, Guayaquil

751d9e0b48ddef49.h:
Sinaloa Cartel - Chicago Cell

Cartels and their cells · United States
Sinaloa Cartel · Mexico

The oldest continuously operating Mexican trafficking organisation, and since the 2016 extradition of Joaquín Guzmán the subject of an internal war between the faction around his sons ("Los Chapitos") and that around Ismael Zambada ("La Mayiza"). Zambada's capture in Texas in July 2024, which he says followed an abduction by one of Guzmán's sons, triggered open fighting in Sinaloa state. Liga da Justica militia

Armed and insurgent groups · Brazil
Rio militias — Liga da Justica · Brazil

The largest militia organisation in Rio de Janeiro state, founded in 1995 in Cosmos and staffed historically by serving and former police, firefighters and prison officers. Its recorded activities are contract killing, land grabbing, arms trafficking, extortion, racketeering, loan sharking and illegal gambling, and it is allied with one drug faction against the others. It belongs on this map because it is the clearest case anywhere of an armed group formed out of the state's own security personnel and then competing with the traffickers it was meant to displace.

A Mhallami network that arrived in Germany in the 1980s as refugees from Syria, Turkey and Lebanon, and which is defined by ethnic and family origin rather than direct kinship. Mundra talc import network

The Mundra talc network · India

In September 2021 Indian revenue intelligence opened two containers at Mundra port and found 2,988 kilograms of heroin concealed inside about 2,000 tonnes of semi-processed talc stone shipped from Afghanistan, the largest narcotics seizure recorded in India. The consignment had been imported by a company founded the previous year by a Chennai couple after earlier ventures failed, and an earlier consignment had passed unnoticed in July. A federal chargesheet named nine accused including four Afghan nationals, describing a network moving heroin from Afghanistan for distribution across Punjab, Delhi, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh.

Directorate of Revenue Intelligence seizure, 11 September 2021; NIA chargesheet, Ahmedabad special court, 2022

Dubai as command and control · United Arab Emirates

The State Department's own assessment is the finding: international trafficking organisations exploit Dubai's position as a global crossroads by using it as a command and control centre and logistics hub, and rising seizures indicate traffickers use the emirates to warehouse, stockpile and distribute. Dubai International Airport became a transit point for cocaine couriers from Brazil bound for Africa and Asia, and for methamphetamine moving from Iran to East Asia. There is no evidence of drug production in the country. What is located here is the management, not the trade.

The super cartel · United Arab Emirates

European police use the term for a set of cooperating organisations that coordinated from Dubai: the Dutch-Moroccan networks, the Irish Kinahan group, the Camorra, and the Balkan Tito and Dino cartel. Arrests in the emirate over five years took in a Dutch-Moroccan trafficker wanted for six killings, a Camorra-affiliated cocaine trafficker, a Panamanian organiser of shipments to Europe, and the Kinahan organisation's alleged second-in-command. The Bosnian leader of the Balkan group was detained in 2022, sanctioned in 2023, and prosecutors accuse him of continuing to direct shipments from Colombia, Peru and Brazil to Europe and Australia from the same base.

c3775422b29017dd.h:
Bissau elite protection network

Networks inside the state · Guinea-Bissau
The Bissau elite protection network · Guinea-Bissau

Academic and investigative work on Guinea-Bissau describes not a captured state but a three-part arrangement: Latin American suppliers, a politico-military elite that permits and protects, and a set of interlocutors who bridge between them. The distinction matters and researchers make it explicitly, arguing the term narco-state implies an institutional entanglement that was not present. The network's undoing came when senior soldiers stopped selling protection and tried to enter the market themselves. At one point about a quarter of Europe's cocaine was estimated to transit the region, a trade worth more than the budgets of several West African states.

US v. Bubo Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y.; Global Initiative and Africa Center analyses of Guinea-Bissau's cocaine politics, 2015-2024

9a77674ae1a233ce.h:
Trans-Saharan corridor networks

Trafficking and smuggling networks · Niger
The trans-Saharan cocaine corridor · Niger

Cocaine seizures across the Sahel rose from an average of 13 kilograms a year between 2015 and 2020 to 1,466 kilograms in 2022, concentrated in Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali; Mauritania alone took 2.3 tonnes in the first half of 2023. UNODC reads the change as evidence of large-scale trafficking through a region whose position makes it a natural stopover between South American production and European demand. Armed groups finance themselves from the traffic, and cannabis resin remains the most commonly seized drug across most Sahelian states.

UNODC Sahel transnational organized crime assessment; UNODC seizure data, 2015-2023

642e06ba88c9444b.h:
Juan Orlando Hernández — President 2014–2022

Convicted · head of state · 2024 · Honduras

Convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to import cocaine and related weapons counts, and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. His brother, a former congressman, was convicted in the same district in 2018. He was granted a full and unconditional US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and released the same day; Honduras then asked Interpol to execute a 2023 domestic arrest order written to take effect if US authorities freed him. The conviction stands and the sentence goes unserved.

Outcome undone: Pardoned by the US president in December 2025; released the same day.

US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y., verdict March 2024, sentence June 2024; presidential pardon 1 December 2025; Honduran Ministerio Publico arrest order, December 2025
Heads of state & family

The office itself, and the families around it. Where a head of state is convicted the trafficking was not something the state failed to stop — it ran through the presidency. Honduras, Panama and Suriname are here; so is a president's son who confessed on television and was never tried.

fa64962db827deb1.h:
Genaro Garcia Luna — Secretary of Public Security 2006–2012

Convicted · security minister · 2025 · Mexico

The cabinet minister who ran Mexico’s federal police during the militarised phase of the drug war was convicted in the Eastern District of New York on all five counts, including continuing criminal enterprise, of taking Sinaloa Cartel payments in exchange for protection from arrest, safe passage for shipments and warnings of coming operations. He was sentenced in 2024. In May 2025 a US court ordered him and his wife to pay Mexico more than .4 billion in a civil suit over public contracts, which is the largest financial judgment attached to any official on this map.

US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., verdict February 2023, sentence 2024; US civil judgment for the Government of Mexico, May 2025
Ministers & security chiefs

Ministers, intelligence directors and service chiefs — including the men who ran the counter-narcotics agencies. Mexico's security minister, Peru's intelligence chief, Bolivia's anti-drug commander and Guinea-Bissau's navy chief were each convicted of working for the trade they were appointed to stop.

3902504c1576c8d0.h:
Desi Bouterse — head of state, later President

Convicted · head of state · 2024 · Suriname

Convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced to eleven years; with no extradition treaty the sentence was never executed and he was subsequently elected president twice. Parapolitica — the Congress investigations

Roughly 30% of the Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the AUC paramilitaries, who were themselves among the country's largest cocaine traffickers. 9263a1f327310256.h:
Vladimiro Montesinos — intelligence chief

Convicted · intelligence chief · 2006 · Peru

Head of the national intelligence service under Fujimori and, in practice, of the military, the courts and much of the press. He was convicted on a long series of counts including drug trafficking, and separately sentenced to twenty years for arranging an airdrop of ten thousand assault rifles to Colombian guerrillas. He was accused of sixty-three offences in all and pleaded guilty in 2024 to homicide and forced disappearance in the 1992 killing of six farmers. He videotaped himself paying bribes, which is how much of the record exists: the agency nominally responsible for counter-narcotics kept its own evidence.

8dfccba4fd6eecef.h:
Edgar Veytia — Attorney General of Nayarit

Convicted · state prosecutor · 2019 · Mexico

The chief prosecutor of a Mexican state pleaded guilty in Brooklyn to a conspiracy to import heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, and was sentenced in September 2019 to 20 years with million in forfeiture. Prosecutors established that between 2013 and 2017 he used the office for the H-2 cartel: directing officers to wiretap and arrest rival traffickers, releasing the cartel’s members from custody, and assisting acts of violence. He had campaigned on the claim that there was no room for organised crime in Nayarit. His governor, Roberto Sandoval, was designated by Treasury two months earlier.

US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., guilty plea 2019, sentence 26 September 2019 before Judge Carol Bagley Amon

2628ea11104a86a8.h:
Tomas Yarrington — Governor of Tamaulipas

Convicted · state governor · 2025 · Mexico

Governor of Tamaulipas from 1999 to 2005 and a presidential candidate, he fled Mexico in 2012, was arrested in Italy in 2017 and extradited the following year. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and was sentenced in March 2023 to nine years, having admitted taking more than .5 million in bribes; prosecutors put the laundered total at between .5 and .5 million over fourteen years. The charges that described the trade itself — conspiracy to import cocaine and marijuana, bank fraud — were dismissed under the plea. He was released in November 2024 after a sentence adjustment for time served and returned to Mexico in April 2025 to face a second laundering case.

60a45e518257b81f.h:
Cartel de los Soles indictment

Indicted · head of state and general staff · 2026 · Venezuela

The US Department of Justice indicted Nicolas Maduro and more than a dozen serving and former officials, including senior military commanders, on narco-terrorism and cocaine importation charges in 2020. Treasury designated the group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in July 2025 and the State Department as a Foreign Terrorist Organization from 24 November 2025, saying the regime had corrupted parts of the military, intelligence apparatus, legislature and judiciary to serve it. 9252b12c2576a767.h:
The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone

Designated · zone granted by the state · 2018 · Laos

The government granted a Chinese company a concession in the Lao section of the Golden Triangle in 2007. Treasury later designated its head and his wife over heroin and methamphetamine trafficking and laundering. The US State Department reported that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations, that jurisdictional confusion between officials and zone security hinders investigation, and that no complicit official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.

598d0759343f56bf.h:
Ruben Rocha Moya — sitting Governor of Sinaloa

Indicted · state governor · 2026 · Mexico

A sitting governor and nine other current and former Sinaloa officials, among them a senator, a state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary, police commanders and the mayor of Culiacan, were indicted in Manhattan in April 2026 over a protection arrangement with the Chapitos faction. Prosecutors allege he met the faction before the 2021 election and undertook to install friendly officials, that cartel members stole ballot boxes and intimidated rivals to secure his victory, and that he then let them consolidate control of state and local law enforcement. He rejects the accusations. Mexico said the extradition request lacked sufficient evidence and opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody. He announced his resignation on 1 May 2026, days after the indictment, calling it a political attack; the mayor of Culiacan stepped down in the same week.

US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026; Fiscalia General de la Republica statement, 2026; resignations reported 1-2 May 2026

4705fa5168743801.h:
The Fourth Criminal Court — Assad and the Fourth Division

Convicted · head of state, division commander and security chiefs · 2026 · Syria

On 11 August 2026 the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced the deposed president to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and his brother, who commanded the Fourth Armoured Division, to death in absentia; six other officials received the same sentence in absentia. Only one defendant was present, a cousin who ran political security in Deraa and had been sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2011; he stood in a cage in prison uniform to hear it and has the right to appeal. Both brothers are in Russia with political asylum and Moscow has refused extradition. Opposition activists accuse the Fourth Division of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, and Western and regional governments treat it as the backbone of state captagon manufacture — but the convictions are for war crimes, not the trade. Human Rights Watch opposed the sentences and questioned whether a fair trial was guaranteed.

Fourth Criminal Court, Damascus, judgment 11 August 2026, reported by SANA and international agencies; US Treasury designation of the Deraa political security head, April 2011; Human Rights Watch statement, August 2026

6cb6ca55911036c9.h:
Nouh Zeaiter — the four-month sentence

Convicted · trafficker sanctioned by the US and EU · 2026 · Lebanon

Sanctioned by the United States and the United Kingdom in 2023 over captagon manufacture and smuggling alongside relatives and associates of the Assad family, and already convicted in absentia by a Lebanese military court in 2021, which gave him life with hard labour, and sentenced to death in absentia in March 2024 for shooting at soldiers, one of whom was killed. The army took him in an ambush near Baalbek in November 2025 and called him one of the most dangerous wanted men in the country. In February 2026 the military court sentenced him to four months, finding him guilty in four minor matters — arms trafficking, shootings, unlicensed weapons and wearing military clothing — with weapons and radios confiscated. He denied trafficking and said he grew cannabis only between 2005 and 2008. The same court that had already sentenced him twice in absentia reached four months once he was in front of it.

Louay al-Yasiri — a governor's son, pardoned

Convicted · son of a former governor, intelligence service employee · 2018 · Iraq

Sentenced to life in 2018 for drug offences, the son of a former provincial governor and himself an employee of the intelligence service. He was later pardoned and released. It is the clearest documented instance of a trafficker with direct government connections reaching an Iraqi court, and the sentence did not hold. Against it stands the volume the same judiciary produces: over 14,000 arrests in 2024, 144 death sentences for international traffickers and 434 life sentences for local offenders, and 973 convictions in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

093621de0215c032.h:
Revolutionary Court judges in the drug docket

Alleged · revolutionary court judges · 2025 · Iran

Defence lawyers describe the courts that try drug cases as security-dominated and fast-tracking low-level defendants while leaving trafficking networks and higher-level operators untouched. One attorney who handled more than seventy drug cases documented the conduct of two named Tehran revolutionary court judges, one of whom he alleges was involved in financial corruption, and submitted a report with case files; lawyers who pursue such cases report being turned on themselves. With no independent forum, the allegation cannot be tested. Iran scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors, the joint highest on this map, and hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.

Center for Human Rights in Iran, testimony of a defence attorney and analysis of drug sentencing, April 2025; Iranian judiciary announcements via Mizan Online

55322fe8dbf41178.h:

Convicted · senior army and intelligence officials · 2020 · Chad

A court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people on 24 July 2020 over a transnational tramadol network, among them high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts reading the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums circulating among its members, some of it used in attempts to corrupt the judiciary and the security services. The conviction is real and the assessment that followed it is the point: with senior army and intelligence figures involved, enforcement runs into the institutions expected to carry it out.

6a89e0e03aa0856d.h:
Tramadol supplied to the presidential guard

Alleged · presidential guard and senior security officials · 2026 · Central African Republic

Reporting from Bangui, drawing on researchers, dealers and a former employee of the group, describes remnants of the Wagner organisation supplying tramadol to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia. Senior security officials are alleged to control the market, in which a consignment worth about $7,000 locally fetches up to $21,000 in Cameroon after roughly $4,000 is paid to Wagner and allied armed groups en route. A US-sponsored research centre assesses that the old Wagner has in effect taken over the state. Nothing has been charged. The country reports no update on an earlier case against a customs agent.

Launching from the empty Hamad desert removed the need for inhabited areas or local help. Jordan intercepted 21 attempts from Sweida between January and July 2025 and 128 more between July 2025 and April 2026, and has struck inside Syria five times since Assad fell, most recently with F-16s against six locations on 3 May 2026. faa0b4cff908af6b.h:
Sweida after the fall

Inquiry · 2026 · Syria

Once a transit route for narcotics moving to Jordan and the Gulf, Sweida became the country's principal drug-trafficking centre after December 2024, with laboratories and smuggling routes held by local armed factions rather than the state. Syria's interior ministry said domestic production was virtually eradicated by late 2025 after raids on former regime facilities, and UNODC recorded fifteen industrial-scale laboratories and thirteen smaller storage sites dismantled within a year; a significant share of what now moves through Sweida arrives from Lebanon instead. Under Assad the model was centralised and industrial, tied to regime and militia structures. What replaced it is smaller, dispersed and harder to reach by conventional border enforcement — 177 million tablets were intercepted across the Arab region between December 2024 and December 2025.

962a58e73b660079.h:
The Canaries-Azores corridor

Indicted · 2026 · Portugal
Mother vessels, mid-ocean transfers and landing craft · Shipping, freight & ports

A two-week operation led by the Spanish Guardia Civil and coordinated through Europol, 13-26 April 2026, worked the eastern Atlantic between the Canaries and the Azores: 11 tonnes of cocaine and 8.5 of hashish seized, eight vessels intercepted, 54 arrests. The method is staged. Mother vessels — container ships, bulk carriers, small non-commercial craft — collect in Latin America and run hundreds to thousands of nautical miles into international waters; cargo moves mid-ocean onto fast long-range boats; a final transfer puts it into small craft landing at remote Portuguese and Spanish coastline. Europol calls these fragmented maritime routes, and the fragmentation is the purpose: no single vessel or party carries the whole exposure. It is the direct answer to the port enforcement recorded elsewhere on this layer — if terminals are watched, the cargo never enters one.

Miami Cocaine Corridor

Trafficking corridor · 13 waypoints

The Caribbean's terminus. Miami's exposure is banking and trade rather than street distribution: the NTR Metals gold case ran roughly $3.6 billion in illegally mined South American metal through Doral, and the city's freight forwarders and correspondent banks are where trade-based laundering resolves into dollars.

US v. Barrage, Granda and Rodriguez, S.D. Fla. 2017–18; FinCEN GTO reporting

f988e9d2af4ee4ff.h:
Balkan Route (Heroin)

Trafficking corridor · 22 waypoints

The principal overland channel for Afghan opiates into Western Europe, running through Iran and Turkiye and then splitting through Bulgaria and the former Yugoslavia. UNODC has tracked it since the 1990s; Turkiye consistently reports the largest single share of European heroin seizures. Its documented capture cases cluster at the Turkish and Serbian ends — Susurluk in 1996, the Đinđić assassination in 2003.

UNODC World Drug Report and Afghan opiate trade series; EMCDDA European Drug Report
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

1978ceeb14be222b.h:
Northern Route (Heroin)

Trafficking corridor · 24 waypoints

Afghan opiates north through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan into Russia. Volumes fell after Russian demand shifted toward synthetics and darknet supply, but the corridor's institutional signature is unchanged: Tajikistan scores 8.50 on heroin against 2.54 on resilience, and senior border and counter-narcotics officials have been repeatedly implicated.

UNODC Central Asia opiate flow reporting; GI-TOC country profiles
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

634cde84932b1f24.h:
Caribbean Route (Cocaine)

Trafficking corridor · 16 waypoints

Cocaine from Colombia and Venezuela through the island chain to Florida and Europe. The dominant route of the 1980s, displaced by the Central American land corridor, and now partly resurgent. Its capture record is unusually concrete: the Dominican Falcón case, Jamaica's Tivoli Gardens enquiry, and the Bahamas' long history of transhipment cases.

UNODC Caribbean reporting; Dominican Operación Falcón 2020; Jamaican West Kingston Commission 2016
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

17b818f7386e75f0.h:
Pacific Route (Cocaine)

Trafficking corridor · 18 waypoints

Maritime cocaine north along the Pacific littoral from Ecuador and Colombia to Mexico, largely by go-fast and semi-submersible. The US Coast Guard's eastern Pacific interdiction statistics are the main public measure of volume; the corridor is why Ecuador's criminality score rose faster than any other country's between 2021 and 2025.

US Coast Guard interdiction reporting; UNODC maritime cocaine research
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

d822ade6bef7e214.h:
West African Route (Cocaine)

Trafficking corridor · 47 waypoints

Cocaine crossing the Atlantic from Brazil and the Andes to the Gulf of Guinea and Guinea-Bissau, then north through the Sahel or by air to Europe. The corridor produced the single clearest state-capture case on this map — the Guinea-Bissau navy command — and the term "narco-state" entered general use describing it.

UNODC West Africa reporting; US v. Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y.; GI-TOC West Africa assessments
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

6288bebd1084e4ec.h:
Southern Route (Heroin)

Trafficking corridor · 27 waypoints

Afghan opiates south to the Makran coast and then by dhow across the Arabian Sea to East Africa, before moving on to Europe or into local markets. The Indian Ocean interdiction record — Combined Maritime Forces seizures — is the main public evidence base. Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique all score 8.00 on heroin.

UNODC Indian Ocean Forum on Maritime Crime; Combined Maritime Forces seizure records
The curve is the shortest path between the waypoints, not a straight line drawn on a flat map. It is not a surveyed track: it does not follow roads or shipping lanes.

2324465de90121e2.h:
Golden Triangle Route

Trafficking corridor · 22 waypoints

Methamphetamine and heroin from Shan State through Laos and Thailand into regional and Australian markets. UNODC assesses the regional methamphetamine market at tens of billions of dollars annually, the largest single drug economy on this map by revenue. Its production zone sits inside territory held by groups formally incorporated into the Myanmar state.

UNODC Synthetic Drugs in East and Southeast Asia, annual

Trans-Atlantic Route

Trafficking corridor · 38 waypoints

Direct maritime cocaine from South America to Iberian and northern European ports. Volume has concentrated into containers through Antwerp and Rotterdam, which is why the corridor's documented capture is port-side rather than at sea: dock workers, customs officers and terminal IT staff.

Europol SOCTA; Antwerp and Rotterdam criminal court proceedings 2018–2024

Historic and current East Asian heroin and synthetic movement through the Pacific to North America. Included with a caution: the corridor's older literature is Cold War-era and much of it has not been re-verified against current seizure data.

Amphetamine and heroin west from Russia and Ukraine through Poland into Germany and the Netherlands. Its institutional signature is customs rather than politics — the EU's external land border is where the capture cases cluster, and they are individual officers rather than ministries.

Trans-Saharan Route

Cocaine and hashish north across the Sahara through Mali, Niger and southern Libya, taxed at each transfer by whichever armed formation holds the ground. Resilience along it — Mali 2.08, Libya 1.88, Niger 2.96 — is among the lowest anywhere.

Amphetamine-type tablets produced in Syria and Lebanon and moved overland and by sea to Gulf markets, principally Saudi Arabia. The corridor is unusual in that the production side is assessed by several governments as state-linked rather than merely state-tolerated, and the destination side is a consumption market rather than a transit point.

Coastwise movement between the Gulf of Guinea ports, feeding the Atlantic crossing. Its capture record is the densest per capita anywhere: a navy chief of staff convicted in New York, a president's son confessing on television, and almost nothing tried in a domestic court.

Light aircraft from Venezuelan and Colombian strips to Central America and Hispaniola. The corridor's signature evidence is wreckage: abandoned airframes in Honduras, Guatemala and Mali, several of which were traced to US registrations through shell companies.

Mexico-US Southwest Border Route

The largest-volume land corridor on the map by value, and the one with the densest enforcement record on both sides. Its documented capture is asymmetric: institutional at the Mexican end, individual at the US end — bought border agents and local officers prosecuted one at a time.

Precursor chemicals from Chinese manufacturers to Mexican synthesis sites. The corridor is chemical rather than narcotic for most of its length, which is precisely what makes it hard to interdict.

Indian Ocean Heroin Route

The maritime span of the southern route, and the one where interdiction data is best: Combined Maritime Forces publishes tonnage and position for its seizures, which makes this the corridor whose volume estimates rest on the firmest public evidence.

Eastern Mediterranean Route

Captagon and hashish moving west from the Levant through Cyprus, Greece and Italy. Cyprus's exposure is corporate — the Limassol company-formation and banking cluster — rather than territorial, which is why its criminality score stays moderate while its laundering role does not.

EMCDDA; Council of Europe MONEYVAL assessments of Cyprus

North Sea Maritime Route

Container cocaine into Hamburg, Bremerhaven and the Scandinavian ports as Antwerp and Rotterdam came under pressure. The offshore leg of the eastern Pacific cocaine corridor: go-fast boats and semi-submersibles running far out past the Galapagos before turning north to the Central American and Mexican coast, rather than hugging the littoral. Arctic Route

Northern maritime movement through the Barents and Baltic. Volume is small and the evidence base thin; it is included because Norwegian and Russian seizure data show the corridor exists, not because its scale is established.

Norwegian customs reporting; UNODC maritime crime programme

Middle East-Caucasus Route

Afghan opiates north-west through Iran into Azerbaijan and Georgia, then to Russia and Turkey. Georgia's 2005 criminalisation of the vory status itself is the corridor's most distinctive state response, and its measurable effect was relocation of those figures to Western Europe and the Gulf.

Georgian Law on Organised Crime and Racketeering, 2005; UNODC Caucasus reporting

Methamphetamine moving by sea through the Malacca and Sunda straits into the archipelagic markets. Indonesian and Malaysian prosecutions reach port and customs staff regularly; the syndicate layer above them, Sam Gor, has been reached once.

Horn of Africa Route

Dhow traffic from the Makran coast to Somalia, Djibouti and the Kenyan ports. Where state authority is thinnest the trade is least concealed: Somalia scores 1.88 on resilience, and the record is interdiction at sea rather than prosecution ashore.

Combined Maritime Forces seizure records; UNODC Indian Ocean Forum on Maritime Crime

Canary Islands Route

Trafficking corridor · 26 waypoints

The Atlantic staging leg between West Africa and Iberia. Spanish interdiction data make it one of the better-measured corridors here, and the Galician clans that receive it are the longest-documented case of local political and commercial protection in Western Europe.

Spanish Guardia Civil interdiction reporting; Audiencia Nacional proceedings

Japan-Philippines Route

Methamphetamine north from Philippine and Taiwanese staging points into the Japanese market, historically through yakuza distribution. Japan is the rare case where the receiving organisation is legally registered and its membership publicly counted.

Trans-Caspian Route

Trafficking corridor · 18 waypoints

Afghan opiates across the Caspian through Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan. Turkmenistan scores 9.00 on state-embedded actors against 2.17 on resilience — the corridor runs through one of the most closed states on the map, so almost nothing about it reaches a public forum.

UNODC Central Asia reporting; GI-TOC country profiles

ec3995e87e7eaac3.h:
Canadian Border Smuggling Route

Trafficking corridor · 14 waypoints

Cannabis and precursor movement across the world's longest undefended border, in both directions. The documented institutional exposure is casino and real-estate laundering in British Columbia rather than border corruption; the Cullen Commission found regulators had failed to act for years.

Cullen Commission of Inquiry, final report 2022

Brazil-West Africa-Europe Cocaine Route

Trafficking corridor · 45 waypoints

The Atlantic leg linking PCC-controlled Brazilian ports to the Gulf of Guinea and onward to Europe. It is the corridor that made a Brazilian prison organisation a transatlantic actor, and the one most responsible for the collapse of several small West African states' resilience scores.

Europol SOCTA; UNODC West Africa reporting; Brazilian Ministério Público

Amazon Basin Cocaine Route

Cocaine base moving by river from Peruvian and Colombian production zones through Brazil to Atlantic ports. River transport is the corridor's defining feature: it is effectively uninterdictable at scale, and the PCC's control of Brazilian export points is what converts it into transatlantic volume.

The record

The only entry on this map where the state itself was the manufacturer. Through the 1990s and 2000s North Korean state entities produced and exported methamphetamine and heroin, moved them through diplomatic channels, and used them alongside counterfeit currency and cigarettes to earn foreign exchange; the 2003 interception of the Pong Su off Australia, carrying 125kg of heroin and crewed in part by a Workers' Party official, is the clearest single piece of evidence, and the vessel was destroyed by the Australian air force after the trial. US Congressional research and successive UN Panel of Experts reports documented Bureau 39 as the coordinating structure. State production is assessed to have declined after roughly 2005, replaced by private manufacture that supplies a domestic market and crosses into China. North Korea scores 10.00 on state-embedded actors — the maximum, shared only with Syria — against a resilience of 1.63. There is no court, no press and no external access, so nothing here rests on adjudication inside the country.

Australian prosecution in the Pong Su case, Victorian Supreme Court, 2003–2006; US Congressional Research Service reports on North Korean illicit activities; UN Panel of Experts on the DPRK reporting

The record

Scores 10.00 on state-embedded actors — the maximum on this scale, shared only with North Korea — and 9.50 on synthetics. Between roughly 2018 and 2024, Syria was the world's principal producer of captagon, with industrial production sites documented in Homs, Latakia and near the Lebanese border, and export moving through the port of Latakia and overland to Jordan and Iraq. Multiple governments assessed the trade as connected to the Fourth Division of the Syrian army and to figures around the president's family; the United States enacted the Captagon Act in 2022 directing an interagency strategy, and the United Kingdom and European Union sanctioned named individuals including Maher al-Assad's associates in 2023. Those are governmental assessments rather than judicial findings, and no court has tested them. The estimated export value, put by several analyses in the billions of dollars annually, exceeded Syria's legal exports many times over. After the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, incoming authorities and journalists found and filmed production and storage sites, which is the first physical corroboration outside intelligence assessment.

Captagon Act (US, 2022); UK and EU sanctions designations, March 2023; New Lines Institute and COAR captagon industry assessments; post-December 2024 site documentation

The record

Scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors, the third-highest figure on this map, against a criminality score of 3.92 and drug indicators that are nearly all at the bottom of the scale. Eritrea has no independent judiciary, no national assembly since 2002, no private press, and an indefinite national service system that UN inquiries have characterised as forced labour. The illicit economies documented around it are human: the movement of Eritrean nationals out of the country, and the trafficking and ransom networks in eastern Sudan and Sinai that preyed on them, in which Eritrean military officers were repeatedly named by UN monitors. A Dutch court convicted an Eritrean national in 2022 for involvement in that trade. Cross-border smuggling of goods with Sudan and Ethiopia is the other significant channel. There is no cocaine or heroin corridor, no documented laboratory capacity, and no drug case against any official in any forum. Massawa and Assab are minor ports. The exposure score here measures an unaccountable state, and nothing about narcotics.

The record

Iran sits between Afghan production and every westward route, seizes more opiates than any other country in the world, and has lost thousands of border personnel in armed engagements with trafficking convoys along the Sistan-Baluchestan frontier. It also has one of the world's highest per-capita opiate-using populations and, since the 2010s, a large methamphetamine problem, some of it domestically produced. Iran scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors and 9.50 on synthetics, against a resilience of 3.08. The documented capture questions concern the Revolutionary Guard's economic reach rather than any adjudicated drug case: the IRGC controls ports, customs terminals and a large share of the informal import economy through affiliated foundations, and Iranian officials themselves have publicly complained about unmonitored jetties. Executions for drug offences numbered in the hundreds annually before a 2017 amendment raised the quantity thresholds, and have risen again since. Hezbollah's Latin American financing, established in US proceedings including the Lebanese Canadian Bank settlement, is the closest the record comes to connecting Iranian-aligned structures to the cocaine trade, and that attribution rests on Treasury designations rather than trials.

The Primeiro Comando da Capital began in a São Paulo prison in 1993 and now operates in every Brazilian state and in at least a dozen countries, with membership estimated in the tens of thousands and a disciplined internal structure that survives the imprisonment of its leadership. Its documented institutional exposure is the Port of Santos, where dockworkers, terminal staff and customs officers have been prosecuted for placing cocaine in export containers bound for Europe, and Guarulhos airport, where similar cases have reached ground handling. Federal investigations from 2023 into the organisation's finances traced holdings in fuel distribution, fintechs and investment funds, and the August 2025 Carbono Oculto operation described a laundering structure running through licensed fuel importers and asset managers on a scale measured in tens of billions of reais. In Rio de Janeiro the Comando Vermelho and Terceiro Comando Puro hold territory, and the parallel problem is the milícias: groups formed of serving and former police, firefighters and prison officers who control neighbourhoods, sell services, and have elected their own members to municipal and state office. Marielle Franco, a Rio city councillor who investigated them, was murdered in 2018; two former military police officers were convicted in 2024 and a former civil police chief and two politicians were charged with ordering it. Brazil's resilience of 5.04 is the highest of the major producing and transit states. In May 2026 the US State Department designated both the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as Specially Designated Global Terrorists, with Foreign Terrorist Organization designations effective 5 June, placing them in the same legal category as Hamas and Hezbollah. The consequence falls on companies rather than the groups: material support is defined broadly enough that a Brazilian firm's counterparties, and its counterparties abroad, carry asset-blocking obligations and criminal exposure for indirect dealings conducted entirely outside the United States. Carbono Oculto had already named fintechs and payment institutions as launderers, so the designation lands on a financial sector that has been identified by an investigation but not yet tried.

A high-price consumer market at the end of a long supply chain, with cocaine and amphetamine arriving through Denmark and the Netherlands and cannabis from Morocco via Spain. Resilience is 7.92 and state-embedded actors 1.50; the institutional record contains no case of an official protecting a trafficking organisation. What Norway does contribute is a policy record that bears on the map's logic: a 2019 government commission recommended decriminalising personal possession and moving responses from criminal to health systems, parliament rejected the reform in 2021, and the Supreme Court then reduced sentencing practice for users on its own initiative in 2022. Overdose mortality remains among the highest per capita in Europe despite an extensive treatment system, a mismatch the commission examined at length. Enforcement exposure is at the Oslo port and airport and the Svinesund crossing with Sweden, and the spillover from Swedish gang conflict into Norwegian cities has been the main organised-crime development since 2022. The record

The strictest drug regime on this map — mandatory death sentences for trafficking above threshold quantities, retained and carried out, with executions resumed in 2022 after a pause — and one of the smallest markets, with a criminality score of 3.72 and a resilience of 7.79. Almost all supply arrives from Malaysia across the Johor causeway and is intercepted at the checkpoints. The country's exposure is financial and it is substantial: Singapore is a major private banking and commodity trading centre, and in August 2023 police seized more than S$3 billion in cash, property, gold, cars and cryptocurrency from ten foreign nationals in the largest money-laundering case in the country's history; all ten pleaded guilty, and the case exposed how family offices and property purchases had been used. It followed the 1MDB flows through Singaporean banks, for which BSI Bank and Falcon Private Bank had their licences withdrawn in 2016. No official has been convicted in connection with a drug organisation, and Singapore's public-sector integrity ratings are among the highest recorded anywhere.

Credit Suisse was convicted by the Swiss Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona in June 2022 of failing to prevent money laundering by a Bulgarian cocaine-trafficking organisation, along with a former relationship manager — the first criminal conviction of a major Swiss bank in the country's history, and the first time a Swiss bank was held responsible for narcotics proceeds rather than for tax or sanctions matters. It is the single most important entry in this jurisdiction. Around it sits a long record: UBS's 2009 deferred prosecution over cross-border tax evasion, the 1988 Lebanon Connection case in which a justice minister resigned after warning her husband about a money-laundering investigation, and the Suisse Secrets disclosures of 2022. Switzerland's own drug policy is the four-pillar model, including heroin-assisted treatment since 1994, which produced measurable falls in overdose deaths and acquisitive crime and is cited internationally. The country is not a transit corridor. Its cocaine indicator of 6.50 reflects consumption; wastewater studies put Zurich, Basel and Geneva among the highest per-capita cocaine cities in Europe.

The record

A microstate with almost no drug trade and one of the most consequential banking cases on this map. In March 2015 FinCEN named Banca Privada d'Andorra a primary money-laundering concern under Section 311, finding that senior managers had accepted commissions to process proceeds for Venezuelan, Chinese and Russian networks, including funds connected to PDVSA contracts. The designation triggered a deposit run and the Andorran authorities resolved the bank within weeks; its Spanish subsidiary Banco Madrid also collapsed. Executives were later prosecuted in Andorra. Andorra then rewrote its financial supervision framework, joined the IMF in 2020, and has since been assessed as compliant by MONEYVAL on most measures. Beyond that case the country's exposure is negligible: cannabis at 4.00 reflects cross-border retail traffic with Spain and France, and there is no production, no port, and no transit corridor. State-embedded actors score 1.00 and resilience 8.00. The entry belongs on the map because it demonstrates that a jurisdiction with no drug trade at all can still be a load-bearing part of one.

The record

The smallest drug market in Europe and one of the highest resilience scores on this map at 8.17. Iceland has no land border, one significant international airport and two commercial ports, which makes interdiction unusually effective and makes the market unusually dependent on couriers; amphetamine and cocaine arrive from the Netherlands and Denmark and prices are among the highest in Europe. The country's most serious organised-crime development has been the establishment of Hells Angels and Outlaws chapters from the mid-2000s, which the authorities resisted openly. Iceland's institutional record contains one case that bears on this map indirectly: the 2008 banking collapse produced criminal convictions of senior bankers including the chief executives of Kaupthing and Glitnir, the only country to jail bank leadership at that level, and the Panama Papers revealed the prime minister's undisclosed offshore interest, forcing his resignation in 2016. Neither involved drug proceeds. State-embedded actors score 1.00 — the joint lowest on this map. No official has been convicted of a narcotics protection offence.

A principality of 40,000 people with a banking and foundation sector that has appeared in laundering and tax matters for decades, and a drug trade that consists of retail consumption. The defining episode is the 2008 affair in which data stolen from LGT Bank by an employee and sold to German intelligence exposed thousands of foreign holders of Liechtenstein foundations, triggering tax prosecutions across Europe and a diplomatic rupture with Germany. The country subsequently signed information-exchange agreements, adopted the OECD standard, and has since been assessed as largely compliant by MONEYVAL. The Stiftung, a foundation vehicle allowing assets to be held with no visible owner, is the structure that made the jurisdiction useful; reforms have narrowed but not removed it. Liechtenstein's resilience of 8.42 is the joint highest on this map and its state-embedded-actors score of 1.00 the joint lowest. No drug case of any kind has been established against the financial sector. The country belongs here as infrastructure, on the same basis as Andorra, Monaco and San Marino.

No production, no port, no corridor, and one of the largest concentrations of investment funds and holding companies in the world. Luxembourg's place on this map is as a jurisdiction where ownership becomes hard to trace: the LuxLeaks disclosures of 2014 showed hundreds of advance tax rulings granted to multinationals, and the OpenLux investigation in 2021 found that a substantial share of the companies in the national beneficial-ownership register had incomplete or absent ownership data, including entities linked to people under criminal investigation elsewhere. Neither finding established a drug predicate. What the record does contain is the country's role as a domicile for structures that appear downstream of laundering cases brought elsewhere, and the European Commission's repeated identification of aggressive tax-planning features in its system. Domestically the drug market is small and concentrated in Luxembourg City; the country opened one of Europe's early supervised consumption rooms and legalised home cannabis cultivation in 2023. Resilience is 7.50, criminality 2.75, state-embedded actors 1.00.
